lessons.title: Greetings for Every Time of Day
lessons.objective: Greet coworkers correctly at any time of day and answer ¿Cómo estás?
lessons.hook: The first words of every call with your Lima team are a greeting.
lessons.explain: Hola means hello and works any time of day. Buenos días is used in the morning, until about noon. Buenas tardes is used from noon until dark. Buenas noches is used in the evening and also as good night. ¿Cómo estás? means How are you?; a common reply is Bien, gracias. Example: you join a 3 p.m. video call and say "Hola, buenas tardes. ¿Cómo estás?" Your coworker answers "Bien, gracias."
key_facts: Hola means hello and works any time of day.
Buenos días is used in the morning, until about noon.
Buenas tardes is used from noon until dark.
Buenas noches is used in the evening and also as good night.
¿Cómo estás? means How are you?; a common reply is Bien, gracias.
angles: Think of the day in three blocks. Before lunch is días, after lunch is tardes, and after dark is noches. Hola fits in all three blocks.
Buenos días is for days, buenas tardes is for afternoons and buenas noches is for nights. Example: a 9 a.m. stand-up starts with buenos días, and an 8 p.m. message ends with buenas noches.
claims: Hola means hello and can be used at any time of day.
Buenos días is the morning greeting.
Buenas tardes is used from noon until dark.
Buenas noches is both a greeting and a farewell at night.
Bien, gracias is a common reply to ¿Cómo estás?

lessons.title: Spanish Sounds You Already Know
lessons.objective: Pronounce Spanish vowels, h, ll, ñ, t and d correctly
lessons.hook: Clear pronunciation makes coworkers understand you on calls, even with few words.
lessons.aside: Spanish r between vowels is a single tap, close to the Hindi र.
lessons.explain: Spanish has five vowel sounds, a e i o u, each short and pure. The letter h is silent, so hola sounds like 'ola'. ll sounds like the y in yes in Peru. ñ sounds like the ny in canyon. Spanish t and d are dental, like Hindi त and द, not like English t and d. Example: llamo sounds like 'YA-mo', mañana sounds like 'ma-NYA-na', and todo uses the Hindi-style त and द.
key_facts: Spanish has five vowel sounds, a e i o u, each short and pure.
The letter h is silent, so hola sounds like 'ola'.
ll sounds like the y in yes in Peru.
ñ sounds like the ny in canyon.
Spanish t and d are dental, like Hindi त and द, not like English t and d.

angles: Read Spanish the way you read Hindi in Devanagari: each letter keeps one steady sound. The e in mesa never glides to 'ay'.
Three special letters to remember: h makes no sound, ll is a y-sound in Peru, and ñ is ny. For example, señor sounds like 'se-NYOR'.
claims: Spanish has five vowel sounds.
The Spanish h is silent.
In Peruvian Spanish, ll is pronounced like English y.
ñ is pronounced like ny in canyon.
Spanish t and d are dental consonants, as in Hindi.

lessons.title: Introducing Yourself: Me llamo
lessons.objective: Say your name, ask a coworker's name and say nice to meet you
lessons.hook: Your first meeting with the Peru team starts with names.
lessons.explain: Me llamo Alex means My name is Alex (literally I call myself Alex). Me means myself; mi means my; the phrase is always me llamo, never mi llamo. To ask a coworker's name: ¿Cómo te llamas? Mucho gusto means nice to meet you. Example: "Hola, me llamo Alex. ¿Cómo te llamas?" "Me llamo Rosa." "Mucho gusto."

lessons.title: Tú and Usted: Two Kinds of You
lessons.objective: Choose tú or usted correctly with Peruvian coworkers and clients
lessons.hook: Choosing the right 'you' shows respect to your Peruvian client.
lessons.explain: Spanish has two ways to say you: tú (informal) and usted (formal). Tú is like Hindi तुम and usted is like Hindi आप in respect level. In Peru, use usted with clients, bosses and older people until invited to use tú. ¿Cómo estás? is for tú; ¿Cómo está? is for usted. Example: to a peer you say "Hola, ¿cómo estás?" To the client's manager you say "Buenos días, ¿cómo está?"
key_facts: Spanish has two ways to say you: tú (informal) and usted (formal).
Tú is like Hindi तुम and usted is like Hindi आप in respect level.

angles: When you would say आप in Hindi, say usted in Spanish. When you would say तुम, say tú.
Listen to the verb ending. Estás, with an s, goes with tú. Está, without the s, goes with usted. Start formal and let the other person invite you to switch.
claims: Spanish has an informal tú and a formal usted.
Usted is comparable in respect level to Hindi aap.
In Peruvian workplaces, usted is the safe default with clients and superiors.
¿Cómo está? is the usted form.

lessons.title: Ser: Soy and Es
lessons.objective: Say who you are, what your job is and where you are from
lessons.hook: Telling coworkers your job and origin needs one verb: ser.
lessons.explain: Ser means to be, for identity, job, and origin. Soy means I am; es means he, she, it is, or you (usted) are. Estu is not a Spanish word; use es for is. Spanish usually drops the subject: Soy ingeniero means I am an engineer. Example: "Soy Alex. Soy de la India. Soy ingeniero. Rosa es analista."

Soy means I am; es means he, she, it is, or you (usted) are.

lessons.title: Mi, Tu, Su: My and Your
lessons.objective: Use mi, tu and su before nouns to talk about your and others' things
lessons.hook: Talking about my project and your team needs these small words.
lessons.explain: Mi means my and tu (no accent) means your (informal). Su means your (formal, usted) and also his, her, their. Tú with an accent means you; tu without an accent means your. Mi goes before the noun: mi trabajo, mi equipo. Example: to a peer, "¿Tu equipo es grande?" To the client, "¿Su equipo es grande?" To answer, "Mi equipo es pequeño."

Su means your (formal, usted) and also his, her, their.
Tú with an accent means you; tu without an accent means your.

angles: Treat it like Hindi तुम्हारा and आपका. Tu matches तुम्हारा and su matches आपका. Mi is मेरा.
The accent is the switch. Tú (you) does things, while tu (your) owns things. Tú eres ingeniero means you are an engineer, and tu trabajo means your work.

lessons.title: Work Words: Trabajo, Reunión, Jefe
lessons.objective: Name the basic things and people at work in Spanish
lessons.hook: You talk about work all day, so say it in Spanish instead of switching to English.
lessons.explain: Trabajo means work or job: mi trabajo = my work. Compañero (male) / compañera (female) de trabajo means coworker. Reunión means meeting. Correo means email (also mail). Jefe (male) / jefa (female) means boss. Example: "Mi jefa es de Lima. Tengo una reunión con mi compañero. Te mando un correo." Tengo means I have, and te mando means I send you.

lessons.title: Estar: Estoy, Estás, Está
lessons.objective: Say how you are and where you are, and choose estar or ser correctly
lessons.hook: Answering ¿Cómo estás? and saying 'I'm busy' happen every day at work.
lessons.explain: Estar also means to be, for feelings, states and location. Estoy means I am (not estu); estás means you (tú) are; está means you (usted)/he/she is. Use estar for how you are: Estoy bien, estoy ocupado. Use ser for who/what you are and estar for how/where you are. Example: "Soy ingeniero. Hoy estoy ocupado. Mi jefa está en Lima."

lessons.title: Hoy, Mañana, Ayer
lessons.objective: Talk about today, tomorrow, yesterday and the morning without mixing them up
lessons.hook: Deadlines go wrong if you hear mañana and think today.
lessons.aside: In casual talk, 'mañana' can also mean 'some time later', so confirm the actual date for deadlines.
lessons.explain: Hoy means today. Mañana means tomorrow. La mañana means the morning; por la mañana means in the morning. Ayer means yesterday. Hasta mañana means see you tomorrow. Example: "La reunión es mañana por la mañana" means The meeting is tomorrow in the morning. "Hoy estoy ocupado" means Today I am busy.

lessons.title: Asking Questions at Work
lessons.objective: Ask what, when, where and who questions with correct Spanish punctuation
lessons.hook: Asking 'When is the meeting?' clearly saves confusion with your Peru team.
lessons.explain: Spanish questions start with ¿ and end with ?. Question words carry an accent: qué (what), cuándo (when), dónde (where), quién (who). ¿Cuándo es la reunión? means When is the meeting? Spanish yes/no questions can keep statement word order and just rise in tone: ¿Está bien? Example: "¿Dónde está el correo?" "¿Quién es tu jefe?" "¿La reunión es hoy?"
